thought.text: Critical finding — the backend build actually **failed** at the `gradlew bootJar` step. Let me read the full log to understand why:

reasoning_content:
Very important discovery! The backend build log shows that the build reached `#10 [build 4/4] RUN ... ./gradlew bootJar` and failed with exit code 1. Wait, no—let me re-read. The log ends with "ERROR: failed to build: failed to solve: process ... did not complete successfully: exit code: 1".

Hmm, wait, that's weird. The build actually failed?! Let me look at the full log. Interesting—but wait, that might be the result of the `docker build` process being killed by the 600-second timeout… no, that's wrong. The error message is a real BuildKit error: the `./gradlew bootJar` process exited with code 1.

Hold on, but the last progress I saw was that the Gradle distribution download was at 60%. Then, after that, the 600-second command timeout killed the process group… and BuildKit reports that the process didn't complete. In fact, if the `docker build` client had been killed, the build should be cancelled, and BuildKit should report "build cache" or "context canceled", not "process did not complete successfully: exit code: 1".

Hmm, but actually—the foreground command that timed out (`docker build -f /tmp/cachetest/Dockerfile1 .`) and the background backend build were both in the same shell session/process group… no wait, each tool command runs in its own shell. But the 600-second timeout kills the process group of that command. The background `docker build` (pid 3328) was launched from a previous tool command, so it should be in a different process group…

No, actually that's not right—the log at /tmp/backend-build.log shows the error. Let me read the full log to check what happened. It's possible that gradlew really did fail with exit code 1 (for example, missing GITHUB_TOKEN… no, the dummy was already set; or a download failure; or a network timeout in Gradle).

Or—did the two builds conflict? The cachetest build was using the same build context (cwd=/workspace/backend) and the same image. BuildKit's build cache is shared. Hmm, but that shouldn't cause a failure.

Wait, actually—I think what happened is this: when the foreground command timed out at 600 seconds, the tool killed the entire process group of that command's shell. If nohup was used to launch the background docker build from a previous command, it would have its own session… nohup detaches from SIGHUP, but the process group remains the same as the parent shell, which has already terminated. When the parent shell terminates, the background process gets re-parented to init. The timeout kill targets the process group of the timed-out command—the cachetest shell, which is a different group from the shell that launched the nohup build…

Hmm, but the pnpm install (pid 3430/3431) is also dead now ("all node/pnpm procs" is empty). That one was launched from a different tool command. So something killed them.

Ah, wait. I got it—the 600-second timeout kill might have used something broader. Or the docker daemon restarted? docker ps -a shows 0 containers. Build cache is 538.9MB.

Actually, let me re-read: `docker images` shows 2 images, 751MB—probably temurin and corretto base images.

The critical question is: why did `gradlew bootJar` exit with code 1? Let me read the full log. It might be the real answer to my token question—for example, a Gradle daemon crash, or a dependency download failure due to the slow network (networkTimeout=10000, retries=0 in the wrapper properties! `retries=0` means a 10-second network timeout with no retries → dependency downloads from the slow network will fail!).

This is important: the gradle wrapper properties have `networkTimeout=10000` and `retries=0`—with a slow network, dependency resolution is highly likely to fail.

Let me read the log.

action.command: grep -n "ERROR\|error\|FAIL\|What went wrong\|Caused by\|Exception\|exit code\|BUILD" /tmp/backend-build.log | head -30; echo "==="; sed -n '/#10 15.59/,$p' /tmp/backend-build.log | head -60
